04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The archivist's answer clarified one small point while preserving the larger uncertainty. Staff had checked the surviving description of the item indexed on 12 October 2011. It had been placed among documents supplied or requested for information about the student travel scheme. The phrase “decision not received” had been entered by newspaper staff. Without access to the underlying letter, the archivist could not confirm whether it reflected the sender's actual wording.

Emma passed the clarification to Sarah.

“So it might not have been a complaint at all,” Sarah said.

“Exactly. It might have been a request for details, or a question about an application. We shouldn't choose a meaning just because one sounds more dramatic.”

They agreed to preserve the archive's description precisely and avoid presenting it as testimony from an unidentified student.

Fiona Bell telephoned later with another fragment of the trust's procedures. An office instruction sheet directed staff to prepare decision notices promptly after a selection-panel meeting. It specified no fixed deadline for dispatch. Nor did it establish when any individual notice had been issued.

“What about the folder of appeals?” Emma asked.

“Still not examined,” Fiona replied. “The team is taking an inventory first. I don't want to promise that it contains completed cases.”

Emma thanked her. The information strengthened her account of the intended administrative process, not her knowledge of its real-world results. The distinction had become almost frustratingly familiar.

She made a chart with three columns: Procedure, Evidence of action and Unresolved. Under procedure she placed the office sheet and decision-letter template. Under evidence she listed reported entries in the dispatch register, carefully marked as not independently inspected. The October index description belonged under unresolved.

Sarah suggested finding a former applicant. Someone who had experienced the scheme might clarify whether decisions were communicated and whether the review option was explained.

Emma agreed, but not by requesting confidential student names from Fiona. They would publish a neutral invitation asking people with direct knowledge of the 2011 travel programme to contact the newsroom voluntarily. Any responses would need checking and explicit consent before publication.

She drafted two versions of the invitation. The first asked whether students had been denied grants. Reading it, Emma realised she had placed an allegation inside the question. She deleted it.

The revised version asked whether readers had applied, helped someone apply or received information about the programme. It did not assume that anyone had been treated unfairly.

As evening approached, Emma forwarded the draft to Sarah with a note: No names without consent, no promise of anonymity we cannot keep, and no claim that an appeal failed.

For once, finding the next lead depended less on an archive than on how carefully she invited someone to speak.
